result.summary: A crow tells Minerva how she was ruined by her faithfulness: she reported that Aglauros opened the basket holding Ericthonius, and Minerva punished her. She then tells how she, Coroneus' daughter, was changed into a bird to escape Neptune's pursuit.

scenes.title: The crow and the basket
scenes.summary: The crow recalls watching the daughters of Cecrops open Minerva's basket. Aglauros untied it and the crow told Minerva, and was banished for it.
scenes.stakes: The crow's place in Minerva's favor, lost despite her loyalty.

scenes.title: Flight from Neptune
scenes.summary: The crow tells of her royal birth and how Neptune pursued her along the shore. Minerva turned her into a bird and made her her companion.
scenes.stakes: Her virginity and life, threatened by Neptune's violence.

scenes.title: Replaced by Nyctimene
scenes.summary: The crow laments that Nyctimene, made a bird for a crime, has taken her place.

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for Minerva, the Roman Athena.
Title for Neptune, god of the sea.

notable_quotes.reason: Sums up the crow's bitter lesson that loyalty brought ruin.
The moral of the tale: chattering birds should beware.

analysis.text: The crow's tale shows that truth-telling can be punished, echoing the raven's fate in the surrounding story.
Metamorphosis is a rescue here, but the divine favor it gives is fragile and easily lost.

fun_facts.text: This Coronis is a different figure from Apollo's lover Coronis, mother of Aesculapius, in the same book.

language_notes.text: Ericthonius was a child of Vulcan born from the earth, not a mother. Pallas (Minerva) hid him in a basket and entrusted it to Cecrops' daughters.
"Two-shaped" Cecrops: legendary first king of Athens, said to be half man and half serpent.
"Actæan" means Attic, of Attica, the region around Athens.
"Placed after the bird of the night" means ranked below the owl, which has taken the crow's place as Minerva's favorite.
"The God of the Ocean" is Neptune, named by description rather than by name.
The virgin who helps is Minerva, herself a virgin goddess, who pities the girl's plight.
Nyctimene was changed into an owl after a crime, in Ovid's account incest with her father. The crow only calls it a horrid crime.

context_notes.text: This crow is speaking to a raven who is on his way to tell Apollo of his beloved Coronis' unfaithfulness, and she warns him with her own story.
Aglauros opens the basket despite the warning. Her disobedience leads to the sisters' punishment elsewhere in Ovid's story.
Phocis is a region of central Greece. Coroneus is her father, a local king.

literary_notes.text: Her loyalty in reporting the secret brought her ruin, a reversal of the reward that faithfulness should earn.
The crow turns her own punishment into a warning against gossip, giving the tale a didactic purpose.
The feathers rooting in her skin makes the transformation physical and unsettling, as the human body is lost.
Repeating hands and breast, first as things she tries to use and then as things she has lost, makes the loss felt sharply.
